chief_complaint: sudden severe tearing back pain, chest pain, and blood pressure discrepancy
hpi_details: A 53-year-old male presents to the clinic with sudden severe tearing back pain, chest pain, and blood pressure discrepancy. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he might be having a massive heart attack or that he severely tore a muscle in his back while lifting something heavy.
concerns: He is terrified that he is actively dying and will not survive to see his daughter's wedding next month.
expectations: He hopes to get immediate strong pain relief and an urgent scan to find out what gave way inside his chest.

investigation_events.title: Emergency CT angiography of the aorta
investigation_events.availability_message: The emergency aortic CT angiography report is now available.

results.value: Intimal flap begins in the ascending aorta and extends through the arch into the descending thoracic aorta; no rupture

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Type A Aortic Dissection evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Type A Aortic Dissection is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Acute Stanford Type A Dissection: Start IV Esmolol, target HR <60, SBP 100-120, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden severe tearing back pain, chest pain, and blood pressure discrepancy

Key HPI features: A 53-year-old male presents to the clinic with sudden severe tearing back pain, chest pain, and blood pressure discrepancy. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Acute Stanford Type A Dissection.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Type A Aortic Dissection.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Myocardial infarction without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Pulse or blood pressure difference between arms; new neurological signs.
management_principles: Plan for Acute Stanford Type A Dissection: Start IV Esmolol, target HR <60, SBP 100-120
Emergent CT angiography (or transesophageal echocardiography if unstable), with immediate cardiothoracic surgical consultation
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of sudden severe tearing back pain, chest pain, and blood pressure discrepancy. HPI: intimal tear in ascending aorta.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Acute Stanford Type A Dissection.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Acute Stanford Type A Dissection.
reference_soap.plan: Start IV beta-blockade and reduce SBP to 100-120 mm Hg while maintaining organ perfusion. Obtain emergent CT angiography (or transesophageal echocardiography if unstable) and obtain immediate cardiothoracic surgical consultation for Type A dissection.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Acute Stanford Type A Dissection
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Acute Stanford Type A Dissection

Implement evidence-based management plan: Start IV beta-blockade with anti-impulse blood-pressure control, obtain emergent definitive imaging, and obtain immediate cardiothoracic surgical consultation

teaching.one_liner: A tear in the aortic wall. Sudden, maximal, tearing pain moving through to the back — minutes matter.
red_flags: Pulse or blood pressure difference between arms; new neurological signs

must_ask.say: Was it at its worst right from the first second?
What did the pain feel like — tearing, ripping?
Did it go through to your back or between your shoulder blades?
Any weakness, numbness, or a cold or painful limb?
Do you have high blood pressure?
Any family history of aortic aneurysm or Marfan syndrome?

history.answer: Doctor, I suddenly felt this agonizing, tearing pain rip through my chest and straight into my back, and I've been feeling extremely weak.
It hit me out of nowhere about two hours ago while I was just sitting at my desk working on my computer.
It was unbearably intense right from the very first second it started, and the severe ache has remained relentless since.
It is centered deep behind my breastbone and shoots straight through between my shoulder blades into my upper and mid-back.
It feels like something inside is physically tearing or ripping apart; it is completely different from a normal ache or cramp.
Yes, it radiates straight through to my back between my shoulder blades, but it doesn't travel down my left arm or into my jaw.
It has been constantly agonizing for the entire two hours without letting up at all.
It is definitely a ten out of ten. It's the most severe, unbearable pain I have ever experienced in my life.
Nothing I do makes it any better. It started when I was resting, and staying still doesn't relieve it.
Taking a deep breath or changing my posture doesn't change the pain at all, and pressing on my chest doesn't make it hurt more.
I don't have any heartburn, sour fluid backing up, or pain when swallowing, and it has nothing to do with what I ate.
I broke out into a cold drenching sweat and felt nauseous, but I haven't thrown up.
My breathing feels somewhat shallow and fast because of how intense the pain is, and I felt lightheaded when I stood up.
I haven't passed out, and I don't have any numbness, tingling, or weakness in my arms or legs.
No fever, no chills, and no cough or phlegm.
No, I have been completely healthy recently and haven't had a cold, sore throat, or body aches.
No, neither of my legs is swollen or painful, and I haven't been on any long flights or had any surgeries recently.
No, there are no rashes, blisters, or skin changes anywhere on my chest or back.
I feel a terrifying sense of dread, like something catastrophic is happening inside my body.
No, I haven't had any chest trauma, falls, heavy lifting, or strenuous workouts recently.
I have never had pain anything like this before, and I've never seen a cardiologist or had any heart stents.
history.topic: Past chest pain and cardiac procedures

history.answer: I haven't seen a doctor in years so I wasn't diagnosed with anything, but at a routine checkup years ago they said my blood pressure was slightly elevated.
I don't have any diagnosed medical conditions like diabetes, kidney problems, or cholesterol issues.
I've never had any surgeries and I've never been admitted to a hospital before.
I don't take any prescription medicines, over-the-counter pills, or herbal supplements.
I don't have any known allergies to medications or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink a glass or two of beer socially once or twice a month, and I don't use any recreational drugs.
I work as an office manager and live with my wife and two teenage children.
My father passed away in his sixties from a sudden heart issue, but no one in my family had an aneurysm, dissection, or tall loose-jointed disorders.
I felt this awful tearing sensation and thought either I'm having a massive heart attack or I ripped a muscle in my back.

The pain is so agonizing that I feel like I'm dying right now, and I just need to make it to my daughter's wedding next month. I just need an immediate shot for this unbearable pain and an emergency scan to see what tore inside me.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 178/96 mmHg in the right arm and 144/84 mmHg in the left arm; heart rate 98 bpm, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C.
Middle-aged male in acute severe distress, clutching his chest, diaphoretic and visibly pale.
Normal jugular venous pressure without evidence of jugular venous distension.
Symmetrical chest wall expansion; no tenderness on palpation of the sternum or costochondral joints.
Normal resonant percussion bilaterally across all lung fields.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with equal air entry; no crackles, rales, or rhonchi.
Tachycardic regular rhythm; a soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur is audible along the right sternal border; no pericardial rub or gallop.
Right radial pulse is bounding, whereas the left radial pulse is distinctly diminished; femoral pulses are present bilaterally.
Abdomen is soft and flat with no tenderness, guarding, rebound, or pulsatile mass.
No pretibial or ankle edema bilaterally; calves are soft and nontender without asymmetric swelling.
Skin is cool and clammy with profuse diaphoresis; no vesicular eruptions, purpura, or erythema.
Motor strength is 5/5 in all four extremities; no focal motor or sensory deficit noted.
